newsitem.title: DENMARK: Britain's Rushdie receives award amid Danish fears.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Rushdie receives award amid Danish fears.

text.p: British author Salman Rushdie, shrugging off official concern that he might be the target of an Islamic assassination plot on Danish soil, collected a European Union literary award on Wednesday at a ceremony in Copenhagen.

Speaking at a news conference ahead of the prize-giving ceremony, he said he accepted the government's apologies for its initial attempts to block the visit but remained sceptical that there was a concrete plan to kill him in Copenhagen,
"I am not convinced, and my information from the other side of the water does not lead me to believe in the existence of any specific threat in Copenhagen, today or tomorrow," he said.

Danish officials have indicated that the initial attempt to shelve a ceremony planned for Thursday was based on warnings from Britain but Rushdie said that British intelligence would have told him if that had been the case.
"I am satisfied that the British did not inform the Danes of any specific threat," Rushdie said.

Indian-born Rushdie has lived in hiding and under guard since 1989 when Iranian revolutionary leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini issued a "fatwa" or death sentence against him for his novel "The Satanic Verses", saying it blasphemed against Islam.

Danish Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen, whose minority government came close to falling as a result of its admitted bungling of the affair, was adamant that intelligence reports indicated a specific threat but said he could not give details.

"The whole question was not only a question of Mr Rushdie but people around Mr Rushdie at the ceremony," he said, adding that Denmark's initial reluctance to host the ceremony was not a concession to Iranian pressure.
"My government and this country never, ever will fall on our knees before the fatwa," Rasmussen said.

"We ask the Iranian government to lift the fatwa as quickly as possible and to issue guarantees that it will not be carried out or sponsored by the Iranian government," he added. "The Iranian government should, furthermore, actively discourage all individuals, groups or nations from carrying out the fatwa."
Throughout the day Danish police guarded Rushdie closely.
Reporters arriving for news conferences with the writer and Rasmussen were searched and their bags were checked by dogs.

Then they were put aboard police buses and driven first to parliament for the meeting with Rasmussen, then to a secret destination, which turned out to be a hotel in the distant suburbs of Copenhagen, for the Rushdie news conference.
The arts complex on the city's outskirts where the evening prize ceremony was held was chosen because of its easily secured position at the end of a spit of land jutting out to sea.

Heavily armed police stopped visitors at two checkpoints before they reached the entrance, a police helicopter hovered overhead and the 500 invited guests were checked and searched rigorously on their way into the auditorium.

Sharing the European Union's 20,000 ECU ($25,450) Aristeion literature award with Rushdie's novel, "The Moor's Last Sigh", was Austrian author Christoph Ransmayer's "Morbus Kitahara". Denmark's Thorkild Bjoernvig took a separate prize for translating German poet Rainer Maria Rilke into Danish.
"I thought it was a marvellous event and not at all dangerous," Rushdie told reporters after the formal ceremony, held in Copenhagen as this year's European Cultural Capital.
At a reception later he mingled freely with guests, looking relaxed and happy, although shadowed by Danish security agents.
"It seems somehow unnatural for the secret police to be protecting a left-wing writer," he joked. ($1=.7859 Ecu)
